tq: Apply the underlying principle to distinguish administrative division from treaty-based federation.

s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the territorial position of Indian States?
o: The Union is indestructible although individual States may be reshaped
Parliament may alter the name of an existing State by law
Indian States enjoy a permanent territorial guarantee against parliamentary alteration
Parliament may alter the boundaries of an existing State by law
x: Indian States do not enjoy a permanent territorial guarantee. Under Article 3, Parliament may alter their areas, boundaries or names, subject to the prescribed procedure.
tq: Find the single statement that reverses the constitutional consequence of Parliament’s power under Article 3.
sec: Indestructible union of destructible states - no right to secede, Article 3

s: Which Article enables Parliament to legislate on a subject in the State List when the Rajya Sabha declares that it is necessary in the national interest?
x: Article 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on a State List subject following a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest.
tq: Identify the Article from the specific constitutional trigger.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: A resolution of the Rajya Sabha under Article 249 remains in force for:
o: Two years and may be renewed only once
The duration of the Lok Sabha
One year and may be renewed
Six months and cannot be renewed
x: An Article 249 resolution is valid for one year and may be renewed. It permits Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest.
tq: Separate the duration of the resolution from the duration of the law made under it.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the effect of a National Emergency:
1. The executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to States.
2. Parliament can legislate on matters in the State List.
3. The President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three are consequences of a National Emergency. The Union may direct State executive action, Parliament may legislate on State List matters, and the President may modify revenue distribution subject to parliamentary approval.
tq: Test the three dimensions of emergency centralisation: executive, legislative and financial.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: With reference to a law made by Parliament on a State List subject during a National Emergency, which one of the following is correct?
o: It requires approval by every State Legislature to continue
It lapses six months after the emergency ends
It lapses immediately when the emergency ends
It becomes permanently applicable after the emergency ends
x: A law made by Parliament on a State List matter under Article 250 ceases to have effect six months after the National Emergency ends.
tq: Distinguish the emergency period from the six-month post-emergency validity period.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which of the following statements regarding financial consequences of a National Emergency is NOT correct?
o: Transfers to States may be reduced or cancelled, subject to parliamentary approval.
The President may increase the transfer of funds to States as an obligatory consequence of the emergency.
The Union may issue directions affecting the financial relationship with the States.
The President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States.
x: The President may modify the distribution of revenues and may reduce or cancel transfers to States, subject to Parliament’s approval. An increase in transfers is not the specified consequence.
tq: Find the reversed financial consequence rather than accepting every emergency-related statement.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Article 19 is suspended during a National Emergency only when the emergency is proclaimed on the ground of:
o: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
External emergency involving war or external aggression
x: Article 19 is automatically suspended only when the National Emergency is based on war or external aggression. Article 20 and Article 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359 orders.
tq: Discriminate between the grounds of emergency for the limited suspension of Fundamental Rights.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which one of the following correctly describes a Financial Emergency under Article 360?
o: The President may dissolve every State Legislature immediately.
Parliament may legislate on every State List subject without further conditions.
The Centre may direct States to observe canons of financial propriety.
The Supreme Court may suspend the distribution of all taxes.
x: During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may direct States to observe canons of financial propriety. Other consequences include reduction of salaries and reservation of State Money Bills for the President.
tq: Ask which authority performs the specified financial function.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Article 360 deals with Financial Emergency. Article 352 concerns National Emergency, Article 356 concerns failure of constitutional machinery in a State, and Article 249 concerns legislation on State List matters in the national interest.
tq: Use Article-number matching and reject the neighbouring constitutional provisions.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A proclamation of National Emergency requires parliamentary approval within one month.
2. Approval requires a special majority.
3. Once approved, the proclamation is renewable every six months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: A National Emergency must be approved by both Houses within one month by the prescribed special majority and may continue through successive six-month approvals.
tq: Combine the approval period, majority and renewal rules in one constitutional sequence.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Parliamentary approval of a proclamation under Article 356 must be obtained within:
x: A proclamation of President’s Rule under Article 356 must be approved by Parliament within two months by a simple majority.
tq: Distinguish the two-month Article 356 period from the one-month National Emergency period.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which of the following conditions is required for continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year?
o: A special majority in the Rajya Sabha alone
A National Emergency in operation and certification by the Election Commission
A resolution of the Inter-State Council
x: Continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year requires that a National Emergency is in operation and that the Election Commission certifies the difficulty of holding elections in the State.
tq: Identify the additional safeguards attached to extension beyond the normal period.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s:
Arrange the following National Emergencies in chronological order:
A. Emergency proclaimed in 1975
B. Emergency proclaimed in 1962
C. Emergency proclaimed in 1971
x: The National Emergencies mentioned were proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975, respectively. Therefore, the correct order is B, C, A.
tq: Arrange the dates from earliest to latest before checking the coded options.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which of the following statements about the 1975 National Emergency is correct?
o: It was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed on the ground of internal disturbance.
It was proclaimed by Parliament after the 44th Amendment on the ground of internal disturbance.
It was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 by the President on the ground of external aggression.
It was proclaimed on 26 January 1975 by the Union Cabinet on the ground of armed rebellion.
x: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on 25 June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance.
tq: Combine the date, constitutional ground and constitutional authority in one precise recall question.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s:
With reference to safeguards introduced or strengthened by the Forty-fourth Amendment, consider the following statements:
1. The proclamation of Emergency must be based on the written advice of the Union Cabinet.
2. Notice by one-tenth of the Lok Sabha members can require a special sitting within fourteen days to consider disapproval.
3. The expression ‘internal disturbance’ was retained as a ground for Emergency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Forty-fourth Amendment replaced ‘internal disturbance’ with ‘armed rebellion’.
tq: Find the one statement that reverses a major safeguard introduced by the amendment.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional significance of Part XVIII of the Constitution?
o: It permits States to secede from the Union during a National Emergency.
It permanently abolishes the federal distribution of powers during every emergency.
It permits the federation to become unitary during specified circumstances without a formal constitutional amendment.
It applies only to Financial Emergency and not to other emergencies.
x: Part XVIII, comprising Articles 352 to 360, enables the federal system to operate in a unitary manner during emergencies without a formal constitutional amendment.
tq: Test the scope and constitutional effect of the emergency provisions together.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: The statement that the Indian Constitution is “federal in normal times and unitary in emergencies” is associated with:
x: B. R. Ambedkar characterised the Constitution as federal in normal times and unitary in emergencies.
tq: Match the constitutional characterisation with its associated thinker.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: The distinctive feature that the mode of operation of the Indian Constitution can change from federal to unitary without a constitutional amendment is described as:
o: A conventional feature of all federations
A unique feature of the Indian constitutional system
A feature created by judicial convention after 1994
A feature available only under Article 249
x: The ability to shift between federal and unitary modes without a formal constitutional amendment is regarded as a unique feature of the Indian constitutional system.
tq: Identify the exceptional feature rather than confusing it with an ordinary federal characteristic.
sec: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Constitution is not truly federal and that the States are not sovereign?
o: State of West Bengal v Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
S. R. Bommai v Union of India
Minerva Mills v Union of India
x: In State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution was not truly federal and that States were not sovereign. The case also concerned Parliament’s power to acquire State property.
tq: Match the case with its specific judicial characterisation of federalism.
sec: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

s: Which of the following correctly represents the holding in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) concerning federalism?
o: Federal character was recognised as one of the basic features.
States were declared sovereign entities with a right to secede.
Article 356 was held immune from judicial review.
Federalism was excluded from the basic structure.
x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) listed the federal character among the basic features of the Constitution.
tq: Use the basic-structure doctrine as the anchor for identifying the correct holding.
sec: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

s:
Consider the following statements regarding S. R. Bommai v Union of India (1994):
1. Federalism was recognised as part of the basic structure.
2. A proclamation under Article 356 was held open to judicial review.
3. The case placed limits on misuse of Article 356.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements correctly describe the significance of S. R. Bommai v Union of India (1994). The judgment recognised federalism as part of the basic structure and enabled judicial scrutiny of Article 356 proclamations, including through the floor-test principle.
tq: Link the case to all three related consequences instead of isolating only the basic-structure point.
sec: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

s: Which one of the following formulations best reflects the Supreme Court’s description of Indian federalism in several decisions?
o: Purely federal with no unitary features
Fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements
Purely unitary with a nominal federal distribution
x: The Constitution has been described as fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements. This reflects the coexistence of federal distribution and strong centralising provisions.
tq: Choose the precise judicial formulation rather than an extreme description.
sec: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

s:
Assertion (A): Federalism is part of the basic structure of the Indian Constitution.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court recognised the federal character among the basic features in Kesavananda Bharati and reaffirmed federalism’s basic-structure status in S. R. Bommai.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the cited constitutional cases directly support the conclusion that federalism forms part of the basic structure.
tq: Check whether the cited judgments directly establish the constitutional proposition.
sec: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

s: The Governor of a State holds office during the pleasure of the President under which of the following Articles of the Constitution?
x: Article 156 provides that the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. Article 155 deals with the appointment of the Governor.
tq: Distinguish the closely related constitutional provisions on appointment and tenure.
sec: Centrally controlled institutions - Governor's office, All-India and central services, audit, elections - critique as violating federal principles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding centrally controlled institutions in India:
1. All India Services are recruited through the Union Public Service Commission.
2. Officers of All India Services serve only the Union Government.
3. The services are controlled by the Centre despite serving both the Union and the States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All India Services such as the IAS, IPS and IFoS are recruited through the UPSC and serve the States as well as the Union. Their central control is regarded as a unitary element; statement 2 is false.
tq: Reject the absolute statement containing ‘only’ and identify the Centre-State relationship.
sec: Centrally controlled institutions - Governor's office, All-India and central services, audit, elections - critique as violating federal principles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the integrated machinery relating to audit and elections in India?
o: The CAG audits Union and State accounts, while the Election Commission conducts elections to Parliament and State legislatures.
The Election Commission audits accounts, while the CAG conducts elections to Parliament.
The CAG audits only Union accounts, while State elections are conducted by State Election Commissions.
The Finance Commission audits Union and State accounts, while Parliament conducts State elections.
x: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits both Union and State accounts. The Election Commission conducts elections to Parliament and State legislatures, reflecting an integrated institutional structure.
tq: Match each constitutional institution with its actual function.
sec: Centrally controlled institutions - Governor's office, All-India and central services, audit, elections - critique as violating federal principles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following institutions is also integrated in a manner that has been viewed as reducing the federal character of the Constitution?
o: Separate Supreme Courts for the Union and every State
Separate Union and State judiciaries with State appointment of all High Court judges
A single judiciary with the Centre appointing High Court judges
State-controlled judicial tribunals replacing High Courts
x: India has a single integrated judiciary, and the Centre appoints High Court judges. These features are commonly viewed as centralising elements in the federal structure.
tq: Identify the institutional arrangement that differs from a dual federal judiciary.
sec: Centrally controlled institutions - Governor's office, All-India and central services, audit, elections - critique as violating federal principles  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of a unitary form of government?
o: Local units being creations of the central government
Local units exercising powers delegated by the Centre
A constitutional division of powers between the Centre and the local units
x: A unitary government does not constitutionally divide sovereign powers between the Centre and local units. Local units derive their authority from the central government.
tq: Find the statement that belongs to federalism rather than unitary government.
sec: Unitary government - characteristics, merits and demerits  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following is NOT a merit of a unitary government?
o: Maximum accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments
x: Uniform laws, quick decisions and a strong response to crises are merits of a unitary system. Accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments is more characteristic of federalism.
tq: Separate the advantages of centralisation from the advantages of regional autonomy.
sec: Unitary government - characteristics, merits and demerits  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following correctly explains a major demerit of a unitary government?
o: It may result in over-centralisation and neglect of local needs.
It gives local units an unrestricted right to secede.
It prevents the Centre from responding to national crises.
It necessarily produces separate laws in every region.
x: Over-centralisation and neglect of local needs are important disadvantages of a unitary system. Such a system may also be poorly suited to large and diverse countries.
tq: Apply the consequence of centralisation to a government-system scenario.
sec: Unitary government - characteristics, merits and demerits  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: India is described as ‘federal in structure with unitary features’ mainly because its system combines federal division with
o: the right of States to secede
equal representation of all States in Parliament
x: India has a federal structure but includes several centralising features, resulting in a strong Union. States do not possess complete sovereignty or a right to secede.
tq: Use the contrast between structural federalism and operational centralisation.
sec: Unitary government - characteristics, merits and demerits  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s:
With reference to the representation of States in the Rajya Sabha, consider the following statements:
1. Seats are allotted to States broadly on the basis of population.
2. The allocation is provided in the Fourth Schedule.
3. Every State has an equal number of seats, as in the United States Senate.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Rajya Sabha seats are allocated to States on the basis of population and are listed in the Fourth Schedule. Unlike the United States Senate, Indian States do not have equal representation.
tq: Use the comparison between population-based and equal representation.
sec: Representation of states in Rajya Sabha - basis compared with equal representation  [GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: United States Senate — representation based on population of States
Every small State — 10 Rajya Sabha seats
Indian Rajya Sabha — exactly two seats for every State
x: Uttar Pradesh has 31 seats in the Rajya Sabha under the population-based allocation system. Small States may have only one seat, while each US State has two Senate seats.
tq: Check the numerical and comparative details rather than the general principle alone.
sec: Representation of states in Rajya Sabha - basis compared with equal representation  [GROUP-II]

s: The unequal representation of States in the Rajya Sabha, unlike the equal representation of States in the United States Senate, is regarded as
o: a federal feature of absolute equality
a unitary feature of the Indian system
x: Rajya Sabha representation is based broadly on population rather than equal State representation. This unequal representation is considered a unitary or centralising feature.
tq: Identify the constitutional implication of reversing the US model of State representation.
sec: Representation of states in Rajya Sabha - basis compared with equal representation  [GROUP-II]

s: A law made by Parliament on a State List subject under Article 249 remains valid for an initial period of
x: A Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 remains in force for up to one year and may be renewed. The law-making authority arises from the national-interest resolution.
tq: Test the exact duration attached to a constitutional emergency-like power.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: Parliament can legislate on a State List subject under Article 250 when
o: two or more States pass resolutions requesting it
a National Emergency is in operation
an international treaty is signed by a State Government
x: Article 250 operates during a National Emergency and enables Parliament to legislate on matters in the State List. Such a law ceases to have effect six months after the Emergency ends.
tq: Distinguish the trigger for Article 250 from those for Articles 249, 252 and 253.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: A law enacted by Parliament under Article 250 on a State List matter ordinarily ceases to have effect after the expiry of
o: the financial year in which the National Emergency ends
three months from the end of the National Emergency
six months from the end of the National Emergency
one year from the end of the National Emergency
x: A law made under Article 250 continues after the National Emergency but lapses six months after the Emergency ceases, unless otherwise continued under constitutional authority.
tq: Focus on the post-event expiry period rather than the period during the Emergency.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 252:
1. Two or more State legislatures may request Parliament to legislate on a State List matter.
2. After such a law is made, only Parliament can amend or repeal it.
3. Every State legislature is required to approve the law before Parliament can amend or repeal it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 252 permits two or more States to request parliamentary legislation on a State List subject. Once enacted, amendment or repeal can be undertaken only by Parliament; statement 3 is false.
tq: Separate the States’ initiating role from Parliament’s continuing legislative control.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: Parliament exercises power under Article 253 to make laws on matters in the State sphere primarily for giving effect to
o: decisions of State Public Service Commissions
x: Article 253 authorises Parliament to make laws for implementing international treaties, agreements and conventions, even when the subject would otherwise fall within the State sphere.
tq: Associate the Article with its distinctive external-relations purpose.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: In case of inconsistency between a law made by Parliament under the relevant constitutional power and a law made by a State legislature on the same subject, Article 251 gives precedence to
o: the State law in all circumstances
the law passed later by either legislature
x: Article 251 provides that the Union law prevails over the State law to the extent of inconsistency. The State law is not automatically erased but operates subject to the parliamentary law.
tq: Identify the constitutional rule governing conflicting Union and State laws.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: Residuary legislative powers under the Constitution of India vest in
x: Subjects not enumerated in the Union, State or Concurrent Lists fall within the residuary field, and residuary legislative powers are vested in Parliament.
tq: Test the authority assigned to subjects omitted from all three Lists.
sec: Powers overriding states - Articles 249, 250, 252, 253  [GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following amendments requires ratification by at least half of the State legislatures?
o: A change in the rules of procedure of either House of Parliament
A change in the representation of States in Parliament
A change in the citizenship law by ordinary legislation
A change in the salary of a Union Minister
x: Changes affecting the representation of States in Parliament fall within the federal provisions requiring ratification by at least half of the State legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2).
tq: Identify a subject that affects the federal balance and therefore needs State ratification.
sec: Amendment procedure - role of states  [GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements about the amendment procedure:
1. Most constitutional provisions may be amended by Parliament alone through the prescribed majority.
2. Federal provisions require ratification by at least half of the State legislatures by simple majority.
3. A State legislature can itself initiate a constitutional amendment bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Most provisions can be amended by Parliament through the applicable special or simple majority, while specified federal provisions require ratification by at least half of the States. State legislatures cannot initiate constitutional amendment bills.
tq: Spot the false statement concerning the initiating authority.
sec: Amendment procedure - role of states  [GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is NOT among the subjects requiring ratification by at least half of the State legislatures under Article 368?
o: Appointment of members of the Union Public Service Commission
Powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts
Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
x: The election of the President, judicial powers, distribution of legislative powers and related federal provisions require State ratification. Appointment of UPSC members is not included in this specified category.
tq: Find the institution or subject outside the listed federal provisions.
sec: Amendment procedure - role of states  [GROUP-II]

s: Federalism is best understood as a system in which
o: all governmental power is concentrated in a single central authority
the Union and State governments share power, each being supreme in its own sphere under a written Constitution
sovereign States form a loose league and retain an unrestricted right to secede
local governments derive all their powers from administrative delegation by the Centre
x: Federalism involves constitutionally divided powers between the Union and State governments, each supreme in its assigned sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
tq: Distinguish the defining elements of federalism from unitary and confederal systems.
sec: Federalism - definition, distinction from other systems, source of India's federal scheme → Act  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a confederation from a federation?
o: A confederation consists of sovereign States that retain the right to secede.
A federation does not require a written constitutional division of powers.
A federation is merely a temporary league of sovereign States.
A confederation always has a stronger central government than a federation.
x: A confederation is a loose league of sovereign States, generally retaining the right to secede. A federation creates a constitutional division of powers between the Union and constituent units.
tq: Use the right to secede as the decisive distinction between federation and confederation.
sec: Federalism - definition, distinction from other systems, source of India's federal scheme → Act  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following statements regarding the constitutional expression of Indian federalism is correct?
o: Article 1 declares India to be a confederation of sovereign States.
The Constitution expressly uses the word ‘Federation’ in Article 1.
Article 1 describes India as ‘a Union of States’.
Article 1 leaves the nature of the Union entirely undefined.
x: The Constitution does not use the word ‘Federation’ in Article 1. It states: ‘India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.’
tq: Test the exact constitutional wording instead of relying on a familiar political label.
sec: Federalism - definition, distinction from other systems, source of India's federal scheme → Act  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The strong Centre in the Indian federal scheme was modelled on the constitutional system of
x: While the Government of India Act, 1935 provided the source of India’s federal scheme, the strong Centre was particularly modelled on Canada.
tq: Separate the source of the federal framework from the model for a strong Centre.
sec: Federalism - definition, distinction from other systems, source of India's federal scheme → Act  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: A constitutional design in which an independent judiciary settles disputes between the Union and the States is important because it
o: gives States a right to secede
makes the judiciary subordinate to the executive
abolishes the division of legislative powers
x: The independence of the judiciary enables it to act as an impartial umpire in Centre-State disputes. This is regarded as an essential feature of federalism.
tq: Apply the role of an independent umpire to a Centre-State dispute.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar supported the use of the expression ‘Union’ in the Constitution because
o: States were intended to possess an unrestricted right to secede
the Constitution established a confederation rather than a federation
the Union was formed through an agreement among sovereign States
the federation was not the result of an agreement among States and no State could leave it
x: Ambedkar stated that ‘Union’ was deliberately used because the Indian federation did not result from an agreement among States. Consequently, no State has a constitutional right to secede.
tq: Test the constitutional consequence attached to the word ‘Union’.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The centralising tendency of the Indian federal system resulting from the absence of a right of secession is described as
x: The absence of a right to secede and the strength of the Union produce a centripetal bias, drawing the constituent units towards the Union rather than away from it.
tq: Distinguish the inward-pulling centripetal tendency from the outward-pulling centrifugal tendency.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which historical circumstances particularly encouraged the framers of the Constitution to adopt a strong centralising design?
o: The prior existence of a fully developed confederation
The aftermath of Partition and the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States
The peaceful integration of only a few provinces before Independence
The absence of linguistic and cultural diversity
x: The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States. In that context, centralisation was viewed as indispensable for national integration.
tq: Link constitutional design to the historical context in which it was adopted.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following descriptions most appropriately captures the debate regarding the nature of Indian federalism?
o: India is a federation with an unrestricted right of State secession.
India is described as quasi-federal or federal in structure with unitary features.
India is exclusively unitary and has no federal features.
India is a confederation in which the Union has delegated powers only.
x: Indian federalism is commonly described as quasi-federal or as federal in structure with unitary features. The Constitution combines a federal division of powers with a strong Union.
tq: Choose the formulation that accommodates both federal and unitary elements.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: K. Santhanam associated the strength of the Union with
o: granting an unrestricted right of secession to States
performing every function, whether or not it belongs to the Union
refusing functions that do not belong to the Union
x: K. Santhanam stated that the Union’s strength lies in refusing functions that do not belong to it. The statement reflects a disciplined rather than unlimited conception of Union power.
tq: Match the constitutional thinker with the precise proposition attributed to him.
sec: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the formation of the Indian and American federations?
o: India followed a holding-together model, whereas the USA followed a coming-together model
India followed a coming-together model, whereas the USA followed a holding-together model
Both India and the USA followed a coming-together model
Both India and the USA followed a holding-together model
x: India is a holding-together federation in which a large country distributes power among units to preserve unity. The USA is a coming-together federation formed when independent States agreed to unite.
tq: Test the central distinction between holding-together and coming-together federations.
sec: India vs USA federal systems - common and differing features (citizenship, lists, judiciary)

s: With reference to citizenship in India and the USA, which of the following is correct?
o: India provides for single citizenship, whereas the USA provides for dual citizenship
India provides for dual citizenship, whereas the USA provides for single citizenship
Both India and the USA provide only for single citizenship
Both India and the USA provide only for dual citizenship
x: India has single citizenship. The USA follows a dual citizenship arrangement involving the Union and the State.
tq: Discriminate between the closely related single-citizenship and dual-citizenship models.
sec: India vs USA federal systems - common and differing features (citizenship, lists, judiciary)

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the distribution of legislative powers in India and the USA:
1. India has three legislative lists in the Constitution.
2. In India, residuary powers are vested in the Centre.
